chunks: As for what was narrated by Muhammad ibn 'Ali ibn Mahbub, from al-Haytham ibn Abi Masruq al-Nahdi, from al-Hakam ibn Miskin, from Sama'ah, who said:
I said to Abu al-Hasan Musa عليه السلام: I urinate, then I wipe myself with stones, and then some moisture comes out of me which soils my trousers.
He said: There is no harm in it.

So it is not contrary to what we have said, that urine must necessarily be washed, for two reasons: one of them is that it is possible that this is specific to a circumstance in which he did not have access to water, so in that case it was permissible for him to suffice with stones. The second is that there is nothing in the report stating that he said it is permissible for him thereby to render salat lawful for himself if he does not wash it; rather, he only said: there is no harm in it, meaning by that the moisture that comes out from him after istibra', and that is correct because it is al-wady, and that is tahir, as we shall clarify later, if Allah the Exalted wills. And that which indicates that water is indispensable for urine, in addition to what has preceded...

key_terms.الِاسْتِبْرَاءِ: the act of ensuring clearance after urination
key_terms.الْأَحْجَارِ: stones used for cleaning after relieving oneself
key_terms.الْوَدْيُ: a post-urination discharge regarded here as ritually pure

ai.seo_question: Does moisture that comes out after urination invalidate purity if one cleaned with stones?
ai.summary: This passage discusses the ruling on moisture that appears after urination when one has cleaned himself with stones. It clarifies that the Imam's statement, 'There is no harm in it,' refers to the post-istibra' moisture, understood here as wady, and does not negate the requirement of washing urine with water for salat.
